I am 68 years old, and after fifty years on this land I do not need a book to tell me what my fields need — though I will say that the agricultural extension course I took in the 1990s taught me to think in kilograms per mu instead of bags per plot, and that precision has paid for itself many times over. My wife and I are the only two working this farm now, so every decision has to balance my back against our budget.

I keep four mu in the wheat-maize rotation because it is the backbone of our food security. The wheat is already in the ground, and after green-up I will give it three irrigations from our well: at jointing, at heading, and at grain filling. Pumping costs electricity, but I know from 1997 and 2002 — both dry springs — that skipping the heading irrigation costs me more in lost yield than the pump bill. I topdress with about 13 kg of nitrogen per mu total, split between the green-up urea and the jointing application, plus 5 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium as base. I use an improved wheat variety from the county station; at my age I do not gamble with saved seed.

The summer maize goes in within two days of wheat harvest, always hybrid seed, and I plant no-tillage into the wheat stubble. There is simply no time for ploughing in that window, and anyway the stubble holds July moisture. All the maize fertilizer — 14 kg N, 5 kg P, 4 kg K per mu — goes in the seed furrow at planting. Two irrigations are enough for maize if the summer rains are normal: one at tasseling and one at grain filling.

My other two mu are stevia, in its third year now. That is my cash crop. I learned early that heavy nitrogen ruins the leaf quality — the buyer tests stevioside content and pays less for lush, watery leaves. So I keep nitrogen low at 9 kg per mu, but I raise potassium to 6 kg because that concentrates the sweetness. I will irrigate four times: now at green-up, and after each cutting. The stand is perennial, so I do no tillage, just hand weeding between rows when my wife and I can manage it. I expect about 260 kg of dried leaves per mu.

For chemicals, I am conservative. Two sprays on wheat — herbicide in early spring and fungicide at heading. Two on maize — herbicide at sowing and insecticide for corn borer. On stevia I spray only if I see aphids, which means maybe once or twice, but I budget for two applications. I have seen too many old farmers poison themselves with casual spraying, and at sixty-eight I am not taking that risk for marginal gain.
